content: 1. Countries with large adolescent populations, high burdens of adolescent diseases, and relatively weak infrastructures face significant challenges in addressing health needs effectively. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) has enhanced its Global Tuberculosis Programme by improving data collection for the annual Global TB Report. This aims to better understand the burden of tuberculosis (TB) and track progress toward the targets set by the UN General Assembly High-Level Meeting on the Fight Against Tuberculosis. These targets include treatment, prevention, and addressing the specific needs of children and adolescents. 3. Countries are encouraged to report TB notifications in disaggregated age groups (0–4, 5–9, 10–14, and 15–19 years) using electronic recording and reporting systems. They should also report the number of children and young adolescents enrolled in treatment for rifampicinand multidrug-resistant TB, as well as treatment outcomes and TB cases among children and adolescents living with HIV. 4. Data on young adolescents (10–14 years) are often derived from school-based data collection systems, which have limited utility in areas with high absenteeism and low retention rates. Programs should review national health data collection systems and incorporate a focus on adolescents, including those out of school, to measure the performance of primary care and progress toward Universal Health Coverage (UHC). 5. Monitoring adolescent health programs involves systematically collecting data to assess program progress. This is essential for guiding efforts, investments, and advocacy to spur further action. Monitoring should cover all stages of program implementation, from inputs and processes to outputs, outcomes, and impacts. 6. The International Health Partnership (IHP+) Common Monitoring and Evaluation Framework classifies health program indicators into five categories: inputs (e.g., financing, human resources), processes (e.g., supply chain, information sharing mechanisms), outputs (e.g., service availability and quality), outcomes (e.g., intervention coverage, risk behavior prevalence), and impacts (e.g., health outcomes, system efficiency). 7. Most global indicators measure health outcomes or impacts, while relatively few focus on inputs, processes, or outputs. Countries should select additional indicators tailored to their specific contexts to improve program effectiveness, efficiency, and sustainability. 8. Monitoring should begin at the planning stage and include baseline data to track progress over time. Short-term data should focus on inputs, processes, and outputs, while outcomes and impacts should also be monitored from the start to establish trends. 9. Adolescent health programs require monitoring systems that account for the unique developmental changes and health needs of young and older adolescents, which differ significantly between sexes. Detailed age and sex disaggregation of data is critical for this age group. 10. Evaluation of adolescent health programs assesses whether goals and objectives are being met. Evaluations contribute to the evidence base for intervention effectiveness and inform program improvements or redirection. They should be rigorous, objective, and go beyond superficial checklists to assess quality and coverage. 11. Evaluations should follow the Development Assistance Committee criteria, measuring relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, and sustainability. Planning for evaluations should be integrated into program planning to ensure adequate budgeting and clear goal-setting. 12. Periodic program reviews should incorporate findings from evaluations, monitoring data, and stakeholder opinions, including those of adolescents and youth-led organizations. These reviews should inform participatory processes to re-evaluate and adjust program priorities, approaches, and targets. 13. Many countries lack comprehensive data on adolescent health indicators. WHO and other entities are working to improve data availability, quality, and use for local decision-making and tracking progress toward health-related Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). 14. Research on adolescent health and well-being is essential to achieve health-related SDGs. Key areas include identifying effective interventions, addressing emerging threats (e.g., harmful digital media use, climate change, pandemics), and understanding adolescent development in diverse cultural and environmental contexts. 15. Research on child and adolescent development has primarily been conducted in high-income countries, neglecting issues unique to lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). This creates gaps in understanding normative adolescent development across different settings. 16. Interdisciplinary approaches and collaborations between academic researchers and applied practitioners are needed to address knowledge gaps. Investments in research capacity, particularly in LMICs, are critical to strengthen programs and policies for adolescents. 17. Research should prioritize inclusion, addressing gaps in gender analysis, disability, and the needs of younger adolescents (10–14 years). Strengthening research capacity across multiple disciplines is likely to yield substantial returns on investment.
